title: Second Epilogue — Chapter 12
paragraphs: From the time the law of Copernicus was discovered and proved, the mere recognition that it was not the sun but the earth that moves was enough to destroy the entire cosmography of the ancients. It might have been possible to retain the old conception of the movements of the heavenly bodies by disproving the law; but without disproving it, it seemed impossible to continue studying the Ptolemaic worlds. Yet long after the discovery of the Copernican law, the Ptolemaic worlds continued to be studied.

From the time the first person said and proved that the number of births or of crimes is subject to mathematical laws, that certain modes of government are determined by certain geographical and economic conditions, and that certain relationships between population and land produce migrations—from that time, the foundations on which history had been built were essentially destroyed.

It might have been possible to retain the old view of history by disproving these new laws. But without disproving them, it would seem impossible to continue studying historical events as the results of men's free will. For if a certain form of government was established or a certain movement of peoples occurred as a result of certain geographical, ethnic, or economic conditions, then the will of the individuals who appear to us to have established that form of government or led that migration can no longer be regarded as the cause.
And yet the old history continues to be studied alongside the laws of statistics, geography, political economy, comparative philology, and geology, which directly contradict its assumptions.

The struggle between old views and new was long and bitterly fought in physical philosophy. Theology stood guard over the old views and accused the new of violating revelation. But when truth prevailed, theology established itself just as firmly on the new foundation.

Just as prolonged and stubborn is the struggle now taking place between the old and the new conceptions of history, and theology once again stands guard for the old view, accusing the new of undermining revelation.

In both cases, on both sides, the struggle provokes passion and obscures truth. On one side there is fear and regret for the loss of the whole edifice built over centuries; on the other is the passion for destruction.

To the people who fought against the rising truths of physical science, it seemed that if they admitted those truths it would destroy faith in God, in the creation of the heavens, and in the miracle of Joshua son of Nun. To the defenders of Copernicus and Newton—to Voltaire, for example—it seemed that the laws of astronomy destroyed religion, and he used the law of gravity as a weapon against religion.
Just so, today it seems that if we admit the law of necessity, we will destroy the concept of the soul, of good and evil, and of all the institutions of state and church built upon those concepts.

And today, just as Voltaire used the law of gravity in his time, uninvited defenders of the law of necessity use that law as a weapon against religion—even though the law of necessity in history, like the law of Copernicus in astronomy, far from undermining, actually strengthens the foundations on which the institutions of state and church are built.

Just as in the question of astronomy then, so in the question of history now, the whole difference of opinion rests on the recognition or nonrecognition of something absolute that serves as the measure of all visible phenomena. In astronomy it was the immobility of the earth; in history it is the independence of the individual—free will.

Just as in astronomy the difficulty of recognizing the motion of the earth lay in abandoning the immediate sensation of the earth's stability and the planets' apparent motion, so in history the difficulty of recognizing the subjection of the individual to the laws of space, time, and cause lies in abandoning the immediate feeling of the independence of one's own personality.

In the first case, it was necessary to renounce the consciousness of an unreal immobility in space and to accept a motion we could not feel. In the present case, it is similarly necessary to renounce a freedom that does not exist and to accept a dependence of which we are not conscious.
